claim.pdf_says: 5)  **Characters permitted in user-defined words.** The following characters have been added.   [printed as ordinary numbered list item 5) of clause E.3.3, in the same run-in bold-lead style as items 1) through 4) and 6)]
claim.markdown_says: ## 5) **Characters permitted in user-defined words.** The following characters have been added.   (specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 48984)
claim.why_it_matters: A numbered list item inside E.3.3 has been promoted to a level-2 markdown heading, so it appears in the document outline as a sibling of real clauses such as 'E.3 Substantive changes probably not affecting existing programs'. Its siblings (items 1) through 4)) are plain list text, so the list renders inconsistently and any outline-driven navigation or section-extraction tooling sees a section that does not exist in the standard.

verdict.reasoning: Independently confirmed against the rendered PDF at 300 dpi. Rendered page 1213 (printed folio 1183) prints the line as an ordinary numbered list item: a hanging '5)' marker at the list-marker column, followed by the bold run-in lead 'Characters permitted in user-defined words.' and roman continuation 'The following characters have been added.', in body-text size. To establish the reference styling I also rendered page 1212 (folio 1182), which carries the real clause heading 'E.3.3 Not affecting' plus list items 1) through 4). The clause heading is typographically distinct - bold throughout, clause number 'E.3.3' followed by a tab gap, no ')' marker, no bold/roman run-in split - while items 1) through 4) are typeset identically to item 5) on page 1213. The one visual difference, that '5)' on p.1213 sits about 0.2 in further right than '4)' on p.1212, is ISO's mirrored odd/even margin: every body line on p.1213 (e.g. the 'Tamil:' block) carries the same offset. So item 5) is unambiguously a list item at the same level as 1) through 4), not a heading. The markdown quote is exact: specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 48984 reads '## 5) **Characters permitted in user-defined words.** The following characters have been added.' The prose text itself is verbatim identical in both sources - nothing is lost, added, reflowed or hyphenated - so this is purely a structural markup defect, but a real one: '## ' injects a phantom clause into the outline at the same level as '## E.3 Substantive changes probably not affecting existing programs' (line 48904) and '## E.3.3 Not affecting' (line 48946). This is not benign formatting: because the heading terminates clause E.3.3 at a heading boundary, any section-extraction pass over E.3.3 truncates after item 4) and silently drops the whole of item 5) (about 530 lines of script names and code-point ranges, Adlam through Zanabazar_Square) plus item 6) and its case-mapping table.
verdict.corrected_description: REAL, with three corrections to the write-up. (1) The kind label 'missing-heading' is a misnomer: no heading is missing. A heading is SPURIOUS - the transcription ADDED '## ' to what the standard prints as an ordinary numbered list item. The fix is to delete the '## ' prefix, not to restore anything. (2) The defect is a PAIR, not a singleton. Item 6) of the same list is promoted identically at specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 49521 ('## 6) **General case mappings.** The following case mappings have been added.'). I rendered its PDF page (1222, folio 1192) and it too is printed as a plain hanging-marker list item at the same left margin as items 1) through 4) on p.1212. Any fix must strip '## ' from both line 48984 and line 49521; grep '^#{1,6} *[0-9]\) ' over specs/ISO_COBOL.md returns exactly these two hits and no others, so the pattern sweep is complete at two. (3) The harm is understated. Beyond inconsistent rendering and a phantom outline entry, the '##' acts as a section terminator: extracting clause E.3.3 by heading boundaries yields only items 1) through 4) and loses roughly 530 lines of item 5)'s Unicode script/code-point table and the entirety of item 6)'s case-mapping table. For COBOL.NET this is material, since E.3.3 items 4) through 6) are the normative record of which Unicode ranges were added to user-defined words and to the general case mappings - directly relevant to the CA26 UTF-16 alphanumeric-repertoire decision.
